reason: The text presents the people of Israel as unified with their leader Saul against the Philistine threat. While the text shows fear and dismay in response to Goliath's challenge (וַיֵּחַתּוּ וַיִּֽרְא֖וּ מְאֹֽד - they were dismayed and very afraid), this fear is directed toward the enemy, not antagonism toward their leader. The people stand together with Saul in the valley of Elah, prepared to fight. When David offers to fight Goliath, the people respond cooperatively, explaining the rewards the king will provide to anyone who defeats the giant. There is no evidence of the people being antagonistic, rebellious, or oppositional toward Saul's leadership in this passage. The only interpersonal conflict shown is Eliab's anger toward David, not toward Saul.
